translation:
...had been averted. But the devotees of God do not choose any of the four kinds of liberation (mukti), because liberation itself is as troublesome as punishment — it belongs to the created realm of Omkar, so that whoever attains any of these four liberations must, when the age of dissolution ends and God recreates the universe anew, come back once more into worldly existence. For this reason liberation has been likened to a dark well, because liberated souls remain bound within the very bondage of that liberation. Therefore it is said in Krishnadas's Parichari:

_Jaiso narak taisi e mukti, jiv abujh jaane nahi bhakti_ (Just as hell is full of suffering, so is this liberation of the Omkar realm; but a soul without such understanding does not know the way — that of loving devotion — to escape it.)

By worshipping God out of enmity, one may still receive liberation from Him, but it is of the terrible, extremely harsh kind called sayujya (absorption into His form). A sakhi tells how the Lord gave Shishupal this harsh liberation of dominion:

_So gali Shishupal dei, chakra kaayo tab shish, te ja samaano aapman, so jan Jivanke is_ (Shishupal hurled a hundred abuses at the Lord, yet [Krishna] kept count of them one by one and did not hold it against him as a disgrace; only when the hundred was complete did the discus take his head — and that very soul was merged into the Lord Himself. Such is the recompense the Lord gives Jivanji's people.)

When Shishupal had given Lord Krishna a hundred abuses, the Lord cut off his head with the Sudarshan discus, and merged the radiance of Shishupal's soul into that very form which is dear to Jivanji as his object of worship, granting him sayujya liberation.

There are four kinds of liberation, and their chief qualities are: (1) salokya — the devotion by which God places the soul in His own abode; (2) sarupya — the second, by which liberation makes the soul like unto God; (3) samipya, the third, by which He keeps the soul within His own sight, that is, near Himself; (4) sayujya, the fourth, in which He merges the soul into His own being. Of these four, sayujya liberation is by far the most terrible — He grants it only to His very greatest enemy. Whoever attains this liberation cannot come out of it for crores upon crores of ages. The Lord told the gatekeepers [Jaya and Vijaya] that they could attain liberation after seven births, but they refused it. Without taking human birth, one cannot attain devotion to Vasudev, that is, Vishnu-bhakti.

Those who do not practise devotion to Vishnu are reckoned as demon-like, and it is they who must undergo this harsh liberation. Brahmins who cling to the worship etc. of Shiva-devotion and other deities, engaging in such ritual observances — regarding the Brahmins among them who are wicked, Prabhudatt Brahmachari wrote, addressing the two wrathful Brahmins whom Chaitanya Mahaprabhu had subdued:

In the time of Mahaprabhu Gaurangdev too, two cruel, base-acting young Brahmins named Jagai and Madhai (Jagannath and Madhav) lived in Navadwip. _Rakshasah kalim ashritya jayate brahmayonishu_ (in the age of Kali, demons will be born on earth in the form of Brahmins). Direct proof of this scriptural statement is seen in the lives of these two brothers, Jagai and Madhai. (Haji no. 413, p.491.)

Even Liberation herself longs to attain liberation and become devotion; therefore it is said:

_Mukti kahat Gopaalso, meri mukti karaay, Vrajraj udi mastak chadhe, mukti mukt ho jaay_ (Liberation herself says to Lord Krishna: O Lord, grant me liberation too — let me come to Vrindavan. If even the dust of Vrindavan should rise and settle upon my head, then I, Liberation, shall myself become liberated and blessed — Liberation shall become Devotion.)

There is a sakhi stating that human birth is favourable for devotion to Vishnu:

_Mata hamare Janki, pita hamare Ram, jug jug maagu Jivna, charan kal vishram_ ||1|| (Jivandasji Maharaj says: my mother is Sita and my father is Ram; age after age, forever, I ask only to remain sheltered at Your lotus feet, in Your abode.)

_Mata pita hamare Jivna, sadhu sadguru Ram, aur kachhu maagu nahi, do charan kamal nijdham_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: my mother and father are the saint and the true guru, and Ram — the saint and true guru are my mother, Ram is my father. Beyond this I ask nothing more; only place me at Your feet and grant me devotion to Your own name.)

_Pita hamara Ramji, mata satvanti naar, jug jug maagu Jivna, ghar manav avatar_ ||3|| (Jivandasji Maharaj says: my father is Ram and my mother is the chaste Sita. Age after age I ask only this — that You take human incarnation and grant me human birth, so that I may render You devotion.)

_Kabir mansa janam durlabh hai, dehi na varamvaar, tarvar je fal jhad pade, so bahorin laage daar_ ||4|| (Das Kabirji says: human birth is exceedingly rare to attain; the body is not given again and again. As a fruit that falls from a tree cannot attach itself to the branch once more,)

so if we waste this human birth in vain, it is exceedingly hard to obtain it again. Therefore, having taken this human birth, one should strive to attain devotion and make the birth fruitful. There is a sakhi comparing this to the tree and its fruit.

_Guru taruvar Govind jal, sevak fal samaan, taavdit laaga rahe, to nipaje niravaan_ ||1|| (The guru is like the tree, and the formless, unmanifest Lord is like the water; the disciple-devotee is like the fruit. If that fruit remains attached, by the stalk of devotion, to the tree that is the true guru — that is, if he keeps practising devotion — he will surely attain deliverance.)

Without accepting a guru, one who worships God directly cannot receive God's grace — just as a fruit draws nourishment such as water through the tree, but if that same fruit falls straight into the water, it can draw no nourishment from it. Only while attached to the tree does it receive nourishment; likewise, without a guru, Govind cannot be attained.

_Guru bemukh jo Hari bhaje, taaka kaaj na hoy, uncha chadhi nicha gire, paai taaka kaaj ja khoy_ (If one turns away from the guru and worships the Lord without him, his purpose is not accomplished; like one who climbs high and then falls low, whatever he had gained he loses along with his purpose.)

If one goes against the guru and worships God without a guru, his welfare is not accomplished — just as, after reaching a high state, if one falls into a low one, then whatever high standing had been gained becomes entirely useless.

_Aadha mata sadhka, jahan Parbrahmki aash, pura mata tahan Jivna, jahan sadguru shabda vishwas_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: if a seeker practises worship by placing his trust directly on devotion to the Supreme Brahman alone, his practice is incomplete; but if he practises devotion with faith in the true guru's teaching, that devotion is whole and complete.)

_Aadha mata kon kaamka, jo paave Vaikunthko dhaam, taathe bhagati bhali Jivna, kabahu sant sangat vishram_ (What use is an incomplete practice, even if it brings only the attainment of the abode of Vaikuntha alone? Better than that — [Jivandasji Maharaj says] — is devotion obtained through the true guru, for then one may also, from time to time, find the joy of the company of saints.)

_Guru bin mala ferate, guru bin dharta dhyan, guru bin sab nishphal gaya, puchho Ved Puran_ (Whether one tells the rosary in devotion without having taken a guru, or meditates upon God without a guru, whatever one does without a guru goes to waste — you may seek the opinion of the Vedas and Puranas on this too, and they will give you the very same verdict.)

_Kabir bichhadanmein dukh hai, jaise fal aur daal, uhaanse bichhada so gir pada, so tarat hi pakde haal_ (Das Kabirji says: there is great suffering in separation, like the suffering between a fruit and its branch — once parted from the branch it falls to the ground, and death seizes it at once.)

_Fal tuti jalmein pada, Khoji na miri pyaas, guru taji Govind bhaje, taahi narak nivaas_ (Khojiji says: a fruit that breaks off and falls into water cannot draw nourishment from that water, and its thirst is not quenched; likewise, one who abandons the guru and worships Govind must dwell in hell.)

_Mathethi guru utre, shabda bemukh hoy, Khoji haal fanfedsi, raakha na sake hoy_ (Khojiji says: if the guru is cast off from over your head and you turn your face from his teaching, Death will search you out and seize you however it pleases, and no one will be able to save you.)

_Durlabh deho manushi, taame durlabh gurugyan, gyani durlabh bhakti hai, durlabh Hari rasapan_ (Gnaniji Maharaj says: human birth is rare to attain, and rarer still within it is the guru's teaching; devotion too is rare even for the wise to obtain, and rarest of all is to drink the nectar of the Lord's loving devotion.)

Speaking of the tree and the fruit, it is said in the Samagam that if a soul, on account of the fault of the fruit and the tree having become separated, takes birth again, it may still obtain devotion to Vishnu; but if it desires devotion out of enmity, how can it attain the highest abode? Such a one attains only the way of Death.

The Testimony of Narsinh Mehta Concerning Devotion to Vishnu

Narsinh Mehta's Witness Among the Vaishnavs of Maryada

Sanaka and the other sages are themselves a form of Kaal (Death); so, although devotion may arise through their company, they become enemies of that very devotion. Jivanji Maharaj has said, in the Das Ang:

_Ahan mite nahin Jivna, Sanakadikso saadh, Brahmaadi rach pach mue, ahan badi upaadh_ ||3|| (Jivandasji says: even in seekers as great as Sanaka and his brothers, the ego could not be erased; likewise Brahma and other gods, though such great beings, became engrossed in this very ego of "I am Brahman" and were destroyed by it. This ego, then, is indeed a most terrible calamity.)

It is said:

_Maina na mai na kahi, daam lage das vees, bakrine mai mai kahin, turat kataaya sheesh_ (The myna made the sound "I am not, I am not," and so its worth came to be only ten or twenty rupees; but the goat made the sound "I, I," and so its head had to be cut off at once.)

Ego is the greatest and hardest of all obstacles; even Sanaka and his brothers could not rid themselves of it. Though he preserved a five-year-old's body through mastery of the yogic power of levitation, his temperament was not truly innocent like a child's — he was in fact deeply learned, a man of knowledge; and "jnaanam bharah kriyaam vinaa" — knowledge without practice is a mere burden; the one who speaks but does not act, his words are useless. Narsinh Mehta's testimony is presented in this chapter to show this. The Lord has kept gatekeepers such as Jaya and Vijaya; Sanaka and his brothers won a victory over their bodies, but such gatekeepers are themselves the very manifestation of ego, and whoever wins a victory in that manner cannot help but develop ego. Therefore the company of those who breed such ego is useless. Narsinh Mehta's testimony tells us whose company one should keep to attain welfare — it must be the company of the Lord's devotee-saints alone, for only they can do us good. His hymn on this is presented here.

(Raag Prabhati Sindhudo)

_Tara dasna dasni nitya sangat vina, bhrashht thay Bhudhara man maru; dushtni sangate dushta drushte kari, shravan kirtan nav thay taru; jire vish paane pela durijan dauhela, vish paan karta tan tej hanse; tuj thaki vegalo teni sangat kare, janam kotitana sukrat harse; jire amritni upama sadhune nav ghate, Rahuni dushhtata nav gai jehene; Prahlade Naradni garbh sangat kari, vash kidha Vaikunthanath tehene; jire char muktitani jugat hai jugati, te mahe tahera nav re ratve; behu kar jodine Narsaiyo vinave, janamo janam tari bhaktiyache_ (O Bhudhar! Without constant company with the servants of Your servants, my mind grows corrupted and impure. From the company of the wicked, seeing with wicked eyes, my ear and my tongue can no longer perform Your hearing and singing of praise. Those base people partake of the poison [of sensual pleasure and intoxication], and by such indulgence their spiritual radiance is destroyed; whoever keeps company with such a person, one far removed from You, loses the merit earned across hundreds of millions of births. Even the comparison to nectar does not suit the saints — it is too small a praise for them — for even Rahu, who once drank nectar itself, never lost his base and wicked nature; yet Prahlad, who kept company with Narada while still in the womb, thereby brought the Lord of Vaikuntha under his sway. As for the various means of attaining the four kinds of liberation, Your devotees have no interest in them at all. With both hands joined, Narsaiyo humbly entreats You: birth after birth, I beg only for Your devotion.)

To say with the mouth "I am a servant of Your servants" is easy, but to embody it in conduct is difficult. Kabir says:

_Kabir das kahaavat sukh hai, mai daasanka daas, ab to sabthe ehi bhali, je paanv talki ghaas_ (Das Kabirji says: it is a pleasant thing merely to say with the mouth, "I am the servant of Your servants." But now, of everything, the best is this — to become like the grass trampled beneath the feet.)

Das Kabirji says: to say with the mouth that one is even a servant of Your servants is easy; but only when the true test of becoming a real devotee arrives — the suffering of being crushed underfoot like grass — does one understand how difficult it truly is.

_Kaheni nishri khaand hai, raheni latta loh, kaheni kahe ne raheni rahe, aisa virla kau_ (To speak with the mouth is sweet as pure sugar, but to live it out in conduct is as hard as heated iron; one who speaks as he lives and lives as he speaks — such a sincere person is rare indeed.)

In the Mahabharat, the words of Virat and Vidur concerning the disposition of a servant are found in the Pandav Gita, verse 21:

_Vasudevasya ye bhaktah shaantastadgatchetasah, tesham daasasya daasoham bhaveyam janmajanmani_ ||21|| (May I, birth after birth, become the servant of the servants of those devotees of Lord Vasudev who are peaceful, and whose minds and hearts are wholly absorbed in Him.)

In the Adi Puran it is said:

_Ye me bhaktajanah Partha, na te janah [bhaktah], madbhaktaanaam cha ye bhaktaste me bhaktaastama mataah_ (The Lord tells Arjun: O Partha! Those who are devoted to Me alone are not, in the fullest sense, [true] devotees. The very best devotees are those who are devoted to My own devotees.)

In the Vishnu Puran it is said:

_Archditva tu Govind tadiyaan archayatu yah, na sa bhagvato gneyah kevalam dambhikah smritah. (Tasmaan sarvaprayatnena vaishnavaan pujayet sada.)_ (One who worships the Lord but does not also worship the Lord's devotees, the Vaishnavs, should not be considered a true devotee — he is to be regarded only as a hypocrite. Therefore one should always strive, in every way, to worship the Vaishnavs [together with the Lord]; for God is deeply pleased above all by the worship offered to His devotees.)

Vritrasur prays to the Lord — Bhagavat, Skandh 6, Adhyay 11:

_Aham Hare tava paadaikamula daasaanudaaso bhavitaasmi bhuyah, manah smaretaasupateh gunaanste, grunaante, gruneeta vaakkarma karotu kaamah_ ||24|| (O Hari! A soul ought to have no desire of any kind, yet I do have one desire — that I may become, again and again, a servant of the servants of those who take shelter solely at Your lotus feet. May my mind ever remember Your virtues, O Lord of my life-breath; may my speech sing Your praises; and may my body render You service — grant me this grace.)

Speaking of the Vaishnavs of maryada in the age of Kali, it is said in the Samagam, verse 51:

_Naasti Vishnoh param saadhyam, naasti Vishnoh param padam, naasti Vishnoh param dhyaanam, naasti muktistva-avaishnave_ ||51|| (There is no goal higher than Vishnu; there is no higher station than Vishnu; there is no higher object of meditation than Vishnu; and the Vaishnavs seek no liberation apart from this.)

Thus the Vaishnavs have no need to worship any deity apart from Vishnu — so why should they worship other gods? Since Vishnu grants no higher station to seek, why should they strive after any other? If they come to regard Vasudev and other gods as one and the same, they will be reckoned non-devotees and will not attain the fruit of liberation and deliverance. In the following verse it is likewise said:

_Naasti Vishnoh param sthaanam, naasti Vishnoh param tapah, naasti Vishnoh param gnaanam naasti, Vishnoh param dhanam_ ||52|| (There is no place higher than Vishnu; there is no austerity higher than Vishnu; there is no knowledge higher than Vishnu; there is no wealth higher than Vishnu.)

The Vaishnavs have already obtained the station that is Vasudev Himself, so why should they go to any other place? They already possess the austerity that is devotion to Vasudev, so what use would any other austerity be to them? They already possess the knowledge that is Vasudev, so why should they put into practice any other, ritual-based knowledge? If they were to act according to such ritual knowledge, they would be called non-Vaishnavs. In support of the devotion to Vishnu stated in verses 51 and 52 of the Samagam, those who earlier copied the Samagam have taken note of verses 26 and 29 of the Bhagavat, Skandh 1, Adhyay 2:

_Mumukshavo ghorroopaan hitva bhootapateenath, Naaraayanakalauh shaanta bhajanti hyanasuchavah_ ||26|| (Those who wish to cross this ocean of worldly existence, though they harbour ill will toward none, do not worship Bhairav and other deities of terrible form belonging to tamas and rajas; instead they worship Lord Narayan and His incarnations of sattva.)

_Vasudevaparam gnaanam Vasudevaparam tapah, Vasudevaparo dharmo Vasudevapara gatih_ ||29|| (The essential aim and fulfilment of every kind of knowledge, austerity, and spiritual path lies solely in yoking human beings to Lord Shri Krishna.)

_Brahma Vishnu Mahesh-aadyaa yasyaamsha lokasaadhakaah, tam Aadidevam Shri Ramam vishuddham paramam bhajet_ (Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesh, who assist the world, are themselves but portions of that very Ram; it is He, the primordial and purest Lord, Shri Ram, whom the seeker of liberation should worship.)

In the Padma Puran too a similar shloka occurs:

_Ramaanna-kti paro devo Ramaannaasti param vratam, nahi Ramaat paro yogo nahi Ramaat param makhah_ (There is no deity greater than Ram; there is no vow greater than Ram; there is no path of yoga greater than Ram; and there is no sacrifice greater than Ram.)

_Vaishnavaah paramo dharmo vaishnavaah paramam tapah, vaishnavaah paramo-aaraadhyo vaishnavaah paramam guruh_ (To be a Vaishnav is itself the highest religion; being a Vaishnav is the highest object of worship; and a Vaishnav is himself the highest guru.)

For a devotee of Vishnu, no mantra, scripture or sacrificial rite is at all necessary — this is shown in verse 53:

_Kim tasya bahubhir mantraih shastraiva bahuvistaraih, vajapeya sahasraischa bhaktau rijyo Janardanah_ ||53|| (For every devotee, what use are many mantras? What use are vast scriptures? And what use are even a thousand Vajapeya sacrifices? Vishnu can be attained by devotees alone.)

Numerous scriptures, Puranas or studies are of no need at all to the Vaishnavs, or indeed to anyone. If one lets go of devotion to Vasudev and takes up instead whatever scriptural rites, Puranic observances or forms of worship, none of it is of any use. In the age of Kali, it is Vasudev Himself who serves His Vaishnavs; that is why He is called by the names Govindji and Janardan.

The Vajapeya sacrifice — in this sacrifice, grain and ghee are meant to be consumed. In earlier times it was performed on occasions of celebrating a victory; later it came to be performed for the coronation of kings or for religious consecration. Formerly, Brahmins and Kshatriyas performed it in order to gain prosperity. Wheat and liquor are used in this sacrifice, and seventeen of each required item are used. As gifts, seventeen elephants or seventeen horses, seventeen nishka (gold coins or a gold necklace), seventeen maidservants, one thousand seven hundred cows, and seventeen chariots must be given; the prince would shoot seventeen arrows. It is said that Brahma produced this sacrifice from his upward-facing mouth. It is a shrauta sacrifice which, according to the Shatapath Brahman, only a Brahmin or Kshatriya may perform; this sacrifice is held superior to the Rajasuya. A necessary part of it is a chariot race in which the performer of the sacrifice must be the victor. In Hillebrandt's view this resembles the Olympic games, though it appears to have developed out of chariot racing; Oldenberg's view seems more fitting — that for Brahmins this sacrifice was a preliminary rite before assuming the priesthood, and for kings, a preliminary rite before coronation. (Najar no. 1, p.133.)

The Muktishastra, p.47, states that the Veda does not prescribe violence. There is a sacrifice called Vajapeya in which twenty-seven animals are killed, and in the Ashvamedh two hundred sixty animals are killed, and their flesh is eaten by all — the Brahmins, the performer of the sacrifice, and the rest of the people.

In verse 53, the word Janardan has been used for God, thereby describing God as the one who serves His Vaishnavs; emphasis has been placed on this word.

Janardan — one who stirs up and agitates the wicked, who causes upheaval among people, or the destroyer of Maya: such is Shri Krishna.

_Janaan-arda yato yasmaat pralayo mahati dvikha, atah samprochyate Vede Janaardana iti Prabhuh_ ||18|| (O Naradji! At the time of the great dissolution, the Lord destroys the gross bodies of all beings and withdraws them into His own being; for this reason His name in the Vedas is Janardan.)

_Janaardanam bhutapatim jagadguru smaran manushyah satatam mahaamune, duhkhaani sarvaanyapahanti saadhayatya sheshakaaryaani cha yaanyabhipsate_ (O great sage! By constantly remembering Janardan, Lord of all beings and guru of the universe, a human being removes all his sufferings and accomplishes every undertaking that he desires.)

Janardan is the 126th name in the Vishnu Sahasranam; on it Shankaracharya has written this commentary:

_Janaan durjanaan adhayita hinasti Sanakadeen gamayateeti va Janaardanah. Janaih purushaarthamabhyudaya-nihshreyasa-lakshanam yaachyate iti Janaardanah_ (He is called Janardan because He crushes and destroys the wicked, or because He grants Sanaka and his brothers passage [to blissful states]; or because His devotees beg of Him the highest human goal, marked by both worldly prosperity and the supreme good — for this too He is Janardan. Because He also destroys the mockery of the wicked, God's name is Janardan.)

Devotees worship only the Lord; they need no other ritual observance, Vedic path, or path of yoga. Vishwamitra states this in the Pandav Gita, verse 43:

_Kim taasya daanaih kim tapobhih kimadhvaraih, yo nityam dhyaayate daivam Naaraayanam ananyadheeh_ ||43|| (For that person who, with an undivided mind fixed on nothing else, ceaselessly meditates upon divine Narayan, what need has he of charity, pilgrimage, austerity, sacrifice, and all such other means?)

Devotional remembrance and kirtan of the Lord are declared the very highest, as it is said:

_Gnaanaat parataram dhyaanam, dhyaanaat parataram japah, japaat parataram gaanam, gaanaat parataram nahi_ (Meditation is higher than mere knowledge; recitation is higher still than meditation; and singing the Lord's praise is higher even than recitation — nothing at all surpasses that singing.)

Therefore it is said in the Samagam, verse 54:

_Tirtham japastapo daanam vratam yagnastato-anyakam, Vasudevah param naam sarve vedyah pravartakaah_ ||54|| (Pilgrimage, recitation, austerity, charity, vows, sacrifice, or anything else whatsoever — all of it is Vasudev Himself; all the Vedas are but the proclaimers of that supreme name.)

In keeping with this 54th verse, it is likewise said in the Bhagavat, Skandh 1, Adhyay 2, verse 28:

_Vasudevapara Veda vasudevaparaah makhaah, Vasudevapara gnaanam Vasudevaparaah kriyaah_ ||28|| (The fulfilment of the Vedas, of all sacrifices, of all knowledge, and of every action lies solely in making people devoted to Lord Shri Krishna.)

In the commentary on this 54th verse, the Samagam states that even beyond crores of pilgrimages, crores of vows, crores of sacrifices, crores of acts of charity, and crores of austerities, the glory of the name of Vasudev is greater still.

Adhyaruji Maharaj says: without devotion to Vishnu, whatever else one looks upon is like reaching one's hand into deep darkness — one falls blindly into a pit. The ultimate aim of the Vedas and all such things is, in the end, only the path of devotion; hence Adhyaruji says:

_Jire amurat raja dhyaarue, ane roop arpe jaano de, ved maarag anusaro, bhakti bhaav man aano de_ (Worship that formless King in meditation, and know too that He offers form [that His true nature is both formless and with form]; follow the path of the Vedas, but bring devotional feeling into your mind.)

That reality of God which has no manifest form at all — such a God should be worshipped, knowing His nature to be formless; yet whether formless or with form, His true being exists in every mode. So, following the path of the Vedas — that is, the path of devotion to the highest reality — one should act; hold this thought in mind, for that alone is true devotion to God.

There is one flaw in the Vedas: through indirect, laudatory language they have tried to steer people toward worship performed with a desire for reward. Therefore, in the Gita, chapter 2, verse 42, it is said that from such flowery Vedic speech, bondage through action is incurred, because the Veda is composed of the three gunas; and so, in chapter 2, verse 45, Krishna tells Arjun, _nistraigunyo bhavaarjuna_ — that is, He instructs him to become free of the three gunas. With reference to this, Adhyaruji says that in following the path of the Vedas, the Veda, through ritual religion, has tried to make people forget devotion to Raghupati. Jivanji has stated this in Gurudev Ang, sakhi 13:

_Ola jhola Jivna, je sadguru diya bataay, karm dharmma raghupati, je vede dharyo chhapaay_ ||13|| (Jivandasji Maharaj says: so that one is not caught unaware and dragged about, the true guru has shown that within ritual religion the Veda has hidden and concealed devotion to Raghupati.)

Jivandasji Maharaj says: so that we do not become entangled in the wandering maze of ritual religion and its ceremonies, the true guru — even while the Veda points toward ritual observance — has exposed how the Veda thereby threw a veil over devotion to Ram; this exposes the Veda's cleverness.

Before devotion to Ram and Krishna, every other kind of worship is like a slave, like a servant, to this devotion. In verse 55, showing the glory of devotion to Krishna, a shloka from the Mahabharat is cited:

_Ekopi Krishnasya kritapranaamo dashaashvamedhaavabhrithena tulyah, dashaashvedhi punaroti janma Krishnaapranaami na punarbhaavaaya_ ||13|| (Subhadra says: a single bow of obeisance offered to Lord Krishna equals the completion of ten Ashvamedh sacrifices. One who performs ten Ashvamedh sacrifices is born again, whereas one who bows to Krishna is not born again.)

This shloka was spoken by Bhishma Pitamaha to Yudhishthir in the Mahabharat, Shantiparva 47.91, describing the glory of bowing to God; a similar shloka occurs in the Shrimad Bhagavat also:

_Naam sankirtanam yasya sarvapaap pranaashanam, pranaamo dukh samanastam, namaami Hari padam_ (I bow at the feet of that Lord, the singing of whose name destroys all sin, and bowing to whom removes all sorrow.)

_Durgasansaarakaantaaraa kupaare vipradhaavayaam, ekah Krishne namaskaaro mukya taantaarayishyati_ (For human beings who run about trying to save themselves in this ocean-forest of worldly existence, so difficult to cross, a single act of obeisance offered to Lord Krishna is itself the means of protection — through liberation, it carries him across this forest of worldly existence.)

There are many kinds of obeisance to God. Among them, this shows how the dandavat, that is, the full prostration (sashtang) obeisance, is performed:

_Urasaa, shirasaa, drishtyaa, manasaa vachasaa tathaa, padabhyaam karabhyaam jaanubhyaam etad-ashtaanga-lakshanam_ (When the body's chest, head, eyes, mind and speech — and also both feet, both hands and both knees — these eight limbs, touch the ground, that dandavat obeisance is called sashtang, the eight-limbed namaskar.)

_Dobhyaam padaabhyaam jaanubhyaam urasaa shirasaa drishaa, manasaa vachasaa cheti, pranaamo-ashtaanga eeritah_ (With both hands, both feet, both knees, the chest, the head, the eyes, the mind and speech — with these eight, the sashtang obeisance is performed.)

Sarvaangai abhivadanam — to offer reverence with all the limbs of the body.

_Nidhaaya dandavad deham, prasaarya charanau karau, baddhyaa mukulvat paani, pranaamo danda-sangyita. Iti dandavat pranaamah_ (Laying the body flat like a rod, stretching out the feet and hands, and joining the palms together like a closed bud — this obeisance is called dandavat. This is the dandavat pranam.)

_Paadau shirasthaa hastau, nikunchya mukulaakriti, manobuddhabhimaanaishcha, pranaamo-ashtaangasangyitah. Iti vihitaih sarvair vandanam ityarthah_ (When the feet, the head, and the hands drawn together in the shape of a closed bud, together with the mind, the intellect and the sense of self, are all offered — this obeisance is called sashtang; that is, it is full reverence performed with all these ordained limbs and faculties together.)

_Mantroccharana-dhyaanaabhyaam, manasaa vachasaat kramaat, padashtaangena bhusparsha taddhai vandan muchyate_ ||1|| (That obeisance offered in due order, together with the utterance of a mantra and with meditation, with mind and speech, and in which the eight limbs touch the earth — that is called true vandana, reverent worship.)

_Baahubhyaam chaiva manasaa shirasaa vachasaa drishaa, panchaango-ayam pranaamah syaat poojaasu pravaraavimau_ (The obeisance performed with these five — both hands, the mind, the head, speech and the eyes — is called panchang, the five-limbed obeisance, because it is performed with these five limbs.)

_Ashtaanga vaapi panchaanga pranaamo purusha shcharet, panchaangam eva naari tu naanyathaa munisattama_ ||4|| (A man may perform either the sashtang or the panchang obeisance, O best of sages; but a woman should perform only the panchang, and not the sashtang.)

Thus pranam is itself a form of devotion that brings about one's welfare.

_Pranamya dandavad bhumau namaskaarena yo-archayet, sa yaam gatim avaapnoti na taam ritushatairapi_ (One who worships God by offering the dandavat prostration upon the earth attains a fruit that cannot be obtained even by performing hundreds of sacrifices — for sacrifices lead only to heaven, and that is subject to perishing, whereas the fruit that comes from devotion through pranam, namely the attainment of God Himself, is imperishable. For this reason the fruit of devotion through pranam has been declared greater even than the fruit of sacrifices.)

The Vaishnav Dharma Ratnakar, register no. 210, p.409, verses 17-18, likewise supports this statement. Adhyaruji Maharaj, in Bhavan Charan 26, speaks of namaskar with still greater fervour:

_Sukhe bhakt seva kare, ane bhakt paraayan dev, namo Vishnu em ochare, ehaj tamari seva_ ||26|| (That devotee who, with joy and love, renders You devotion, becomes wholly absorbed in devotion to his chosen deity, and utters "Namo Vishnu" — this alone is your true devotion.)

Whatever any being worships, and whosever devotion it may be, it ultimately reaches God alone — "all obeisance offered to any deity finally goes to Keshav." The final aim of the whole of the Vedas, the Puranas and all such texts is, in the end, only the attainment of God; but between the fool and the learned man, the difference lies only in understanding. The learned man does not err; but if the unlearned man errs and foolishly cries "obeisance to Vasudev," God forgives even that error and looks only at the sincerity behind it.

The shloka concerning "namo Vishnu" is that of Gargacharya, in the Pandav Gita, verse 63:

_Kim taasya bahubhir mantyair bhaktir yasya Janardane, namo Naaraayanaayeti mantrah sarvaartha-saadhakah_ ||63|| (For that devotee in whom devotion to Lord Janardan has already awakened, what need has he of many mantras thereafter? The mantra "Namo Narayanaya" alone accomplishes every purpose.)

For example, among the community of devotees there is a custom of offering pranam after the aarti. What sakhis our elders would recite in their minds while offering pranam, in earlier times, is recorded in the Gaddi Library, vol. 10, p.193:

_Aadne anek tun, sthaavar jangam taahaara tej, tun guruone taahaar, naam, sakal santsu tuj paranaam_ ||1|| (Sakhi) _Indri tana aparaadh, paranaame paachha fare, garath vaa laage kaain, moorakh man saanso kare_ ||1|| _Vinati hai nij daaski, suneeo deen dayaal, gaas aapno jaanke, sadguru hohu kripaal_ ||2|| _Bahu bandhanmein baandhiaa, ek bichaaraa jeev, apne bal chhoote nahin, jo na chhodaavo piu_ ||3|| _Main sevak hu samarthka, kabahu na haae akaaj, jo pativrataa naagi rahe, toh patiku laaj_ ||4|| (In the Aharnish Raas, Adhyaruji says: O Lord! From the very beginning until now, You alone pervade this entire universe; in every moving and unmoving thing, it is Your very essence that shines forth. You alone are great, and Your name is great; I offer pranam to You, together with all the saints. Whatever sins our senses may have committed, the whole burden of those sins is lifted from our heads by offering pranam, and the sins are erased. Offering pranam to God costs nothing at all, and yet foolish people, out of doubt and suspicion in their minds, remain unbelieving about the matter of pranam. O Lord, this is the plea of Your devotee: hear me, O God who shows grace to humble devotees — knowing me to be Your servant, O true guru, show Your grace upon me. O Lord!
